newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Albania's exiled king watching and waiting.
newsitem.headline: Albania's exiled king watching and waiting.

text.p: Albania's exiled king was assessing the situation in his troubled homeland hour by hour on on Wednesday, prepared to return at any time if he judged the right moment had come.

King Leka told Reuters he would go home at once if embattled President Sali Berisha resigned, as demanded by some of armed insurgents despite the appointment of a national unity government on Tuesday.
"I am assessing it hourly," Leka said. "I could be in Tirana within 24 hours of a decision. But I don't want to precipitate a civil war myself."
He was only ready to go to Albania if he judged he could work with the new government to achieve a peaceful solution, or if Berisha bowed to demands to quit.
"I am really waiting at the moment to see just how far these discussions are going, because they are continuing," he said.

"I don't think it has reached the proportions of civil war..but we must at all costs avoid a civil war. We must avoid a war between North and South," Leka added in an interview at his ranch-style home outside Johannesburg.

Premier Bashkim Fino, of the opposition Socialist Party, flew in from the rebel-held southern town of Gjirokaster on Tuesday night and opened talks on Wednesday with beleaguered President Sali Berisha and political party leaders.

In a call for reconciliation, the 34-year-old premier said: "We will aim for understanding throughout the country so that all people embrace each other rather than confront each other with arms and tanks."

The appointment of a premier from the main opposition party, and from the south of the country now almost totally in rebel hands, was seen as a major concession by Berisha as he struggles to restore order.
The exiled king said some breakaway communities were "looking around for a possible unifying factor, and at this moment they seem to think I am the only possibly unifying factor".
As declarations of support came in, pins marking potential pro-monarchy strongholds were spreading over a constantly updated map of Albania in his "centre of communications".

Berisha has said he is prepared to hold a referendum on a return to monarchy, as requested by Leka's supporters in Albania, but it is questionable how much support the king would have in a country he left at childhood nearly 57 years ago.
Leka said the referendum should come before elections in June, rather than the other way around as proposed.

"There are certain elements within the Socialist Party that demand they go together, or preferably the elections go first, because they feel that they would have a very strong grouping in the new parliament," he said.
"Should the referendum go for the monarchy I would have very great difficulty working with a parliament that is under Socialist control."

Leka desrcibed the unrest in Albania as partly civil disobedience, partly mob rule. "There are lots of armed bands who have no political axe to grind. They are simply out to loot. Some of them are fighting each other."
